analysis.title: National Economic Outlook, October 2026
key_insights: PNC expects real GDP growth of 2.5% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027 (Q4/Q4). Q3 2026 GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace, bringing year-to-date growth to 2.7%.
Growth rests on two forces: an AI-driven capex boom and a resilient consumer. Consumer spending accounts for over two-thirds of 2026 growth.

Business fixed investment has grown at a 10.5% annualized pace through the first three quarters of 2026. AI-related business capex has risen at an average 22.5% annualized pace. Non-AI investment rose at a 5.0% annualized pace over the past two quarters.
Much AI capex goes to imported chips and servers, which are subtracted in headline GDP. Capital goods imports are up 60% over the past year, more than twice the increase at any point since 1985.

Household balance sheets are strong. Real consumer debt is still below 2019 levels, net interest expense is low relative to income, and there is less floating-rate debt. Households are also drawing on equity and housing wealth, especially older households, to fund spending.
PNC expects consumer spending growth to slow to roughly 2% real through 2027 as the fiscal boost from larger tax refunds fades. Households may now be more sensitive to asset price swings.

The labor market is low-hire, low-fire. Payrolls have averaged 68k a month in 2026, and the unemployment rate is down 0.3 percentage points from last November's peak. PNC expects job growth of 50k-75k a month through 2027 and unemployment near 4.3%.

Continuing jobless claims are down 13% y/y in late October and initial claims are near record lows. Slower labor supply growth, partly from weaker net immigration, lowers the job growth needed to hold unemployment steady.

Trend core inflation has been stuck near 3% since early 2024 and began re-accelerating in 2026. Shelter is the only major component back at a level consistent with the Fed's target. Services ex-shelter inflation is elevated, which PNC attributes to demand that is too strong.

Core goods inflation remains high because of tariffs from early 2025 and pass-through from higher diesel and energy costs tied to the war in Iran. PNC expects the energy supply shock to begin fading in 2027.
PNC expects two more 25 bp Fed hikes, in December 2026 and March 2027, at roughly every other meeting. It sees the risk as more hikes or a longer restrictive period, not an earlier end to tightening.
PNC expects tightening to work increasingly through financial conditions and wealth effects, which makes equity prices an important channel for Fed policy.

The biggest risk is an equity correction. It would hit both capex and consumer spending, which PNC calls a 'two-birds-one-stone' shock. Household wealth is highly concentrated in equities, and equities are concentrated in a few AI-linked companies.

Other risks are rising long-term interest rates, which could tighten financial conditions without further hikes, and continued disruption in global energy markets, which could keep inflation high while cutting real incomes.
Residential investment is unlikely to improve while the Fed is hiking. PNC forecasts it down 2.4% in 2026 and up 0.6% in 2027.

sector_views.rationale: PNC says residential investment is unlikely to improve much while the Fed is hiking. It forecasts the 30-year mortgage rate at 7.1% in Q4 2026.
AI-related capex is growing at an average 22.5% annualized pace in 2026, and PNC expects business capex to contribute meaningfully to growth through 2027.

PNC expects growth to slow modestly in 2027 as consumer spending and capex growth moderate.
Core PCE stays near 3% through Q1 2027 before easing toward the 2% target.
Unemployment is expected to stay near current levels despite weak job growth.

Q3 2026 level in the summary table, before the expected December hike.

risk_factors: An equity market correction would hit consumer spending through the wealth effect and slow the AI capex buildout.
Rising long-term interest rates could tighten financial conditions without further Fed hikes and weigh on housing, business investment and consumer spending.
Continued disruption in global energy markets could keep inflation high while lowering real household incomes.
Persistent inflation and economic resilience could force more Fed hikes or a longer restrictive period.
The Fed needs to tighten financial conditions without triggering a large equity correction.
charts_described: Figure 1 shows Q3 2026 real GDP growth of 3.4%, with consumer spending contributing 2.5pp, business fixed investment 1.8pp, inventories 1.6pp, government 0.9pp, residential -0.1pp and net exports -3.3pp.
Figure 3 shows capital goods imports up 60% y/y, the highest reading since 1985 on the chart.
Figure 2 shows real non-residential fixed investment up 10.5% in 2026 year to date.
vol_and_positioning: Household wealth has never been so concentrated in equities, and equities are rarely this concentrated in a few AI-linked companies. PNC flags this as the main downside risk.
Older households (boomers and older) show rising net inflows from brokerage accounts into checking accounts, according to internal PNC data, which suggests they are selling assets to fund spending.
geopolitical: The war in Iran is cited as raising diesel and energy costs, which feeds into core goods inflation.
Large-scale tariffs implemented in early 2025 are still keeping goods inflation elevated. PNC says tariff and trade policy uncertainty has declined.

tension_points.theme: equity correction versus capex and consumer
tension_points.bull_case: Consumers keep spending on strong balance sheets and wealth gains, and AI capex keeps adding to growth, supporting 2.5% growth in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027.
tension_points.bear_case: A large equity correction would cut household wealth and slow the AI buildout together, hitting both pillars of growth. Household wealth is highly concentrated in equities and in a few AI-linked companies.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A significant correction in equity prices, or a continued rise in long-term interest rates that tightens financial conditions.

tension_points.bull_case: PNC expects a measured pace, with hikes in December and March, and the Fed has room to move slowly.
tension_points.bear_case: Persistent inflation and resilient growth may require more hikes or a longer restrictive period.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Core inflation failing to move back toward target by early 2027 would point to more hikes than the two PNC expects.

theme_stances.key_argument: Inflation has been above target for nearly six years and the labor market has stabilized, so further hikes are warranted at a measured pace.
A large equity correction would hit both consumer spending and the AI capex boom.
AI-related capex is a major driver of growth and could be one of the largest capex cycles of our lifetimes.
